Chemotherapy-induced dysgeusia

In a 112-person sham-controlled trial during breast-cancer chemotherapy, PBM reduced subjective and objective taste loss and improved quality of life. A later 180-person trial found combined red and infrared PBM outperformed either wavelength alone, but did not include a sham or no-treatment group.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In a 112-person sham-controlled trial during breast-cancer chemotherapy, PBM reduced subjective and objective taste loss and improved quality of life. A later 180-person trial found combined red and infrared PBM outperformed either wavelength alone, but did not include a sham or no-treatment group.

Summary of the Evidence

The indication maps to four unique titles from the oral dysgeusia category after excluding a long-COVID trial that does not concern cancer treatment. Two randomized trials from the same research group provide the principal clinical evidence; two smaller case-based publications add limited descriptive information. The two trials are separate participant cohorts, not repeated reports of one cohort. No animal or laboratory evidence was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

Malta and colleagues randomized 112 women receiving doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide chemotherapy for breast cancer to PBM or sham in a triple-blind trial. PBM was associated with lower subjective and objective taste loss and better quality-of-life scores. A 2025 phase III randomized triple-blind trial enrolled 180 patients and compared red, infrared, and combined red-plus-infrared treatment. The combined regimen performed better than either wavelength alone, but the trial lacked a sham or untreated arm and therefore does not estimate benefit over no PBM (Malta et al. 2022 Malta et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell, tissue, or taste-receptor experiment was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2022 trial applied 660 nm red and 808 nm near-infrared light to points on the tongue during chemotherapy cycles. The later study compared red-only, infrared-only, and combined red-plus-infrared protocols. These results concern taste outcomes during breast-cancer chemotherapy and should not be generalized to dysgeusia from other causes. Detailed settings not verified in the article are not supplied here.

Interpretation

The sham-controlled result supports a possible reduction in chemotherapy-related taste dysfunction. The later active-comparison trial supports the combined regimen relative to either wavelength alone, while the absence of a sham arm and independent replication limits the comparative conclusion.

Evidence strength in source summaryTaste outcomes during breast-cancer chemotherapy after red and infrared PBM: Low Comparative benefit of one wavelength alone: Very low
Publications and records4 unique mapped titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two randomized trials from the same research group provide the main evidence. The 2022 sham-controlled study reported less taste dysfunction, while the 2025 phase III comparison found combined red and infrared treatment performed better than either wavelength alone but had no sham arm. Independent replication and longer follow-up would strengthen conclusions.
